cards.title: Near-linear constant-factor minimum-degree spanning trees
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic algorithm \(A\), absolute constants \(K,C\ge1\), and an integer \(b\ge0\) such that, for every connected simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\) with \(n\ge2\) and \(m=|E|\), the algorithm outputs a spanning tree \(T\subseteq G\) satisfying \(\Delta(T)\le K\Delta^\star(G)\) in at most \(C(m+n)(\log_2(n+2))^b\) word-RAM operations? Here \(\Delta(T)=\max_{v\in[n]}\deg_T(v)\) and \(\Delta^\star(G)=\min\{\Delta(T):T\text{ is a spanning tree of }G\}\). All constants and the program must be independent of the graph. This is a static construction problem; the graph is supplied once, and no update sequence is part of the input.
cards.why: A low-degree spanning tree supplies a connected backbone while limiting the largest number of connections handled by one vertex. A constant approximation in near-linear time would make a strong structural guarantee available at a cost close to reading the graph. The target is substantially weaker than exact degree minimization, but stronger than bounds whose approximation grows with the graph size. This is a static construction frontier, despite the dynamic setting of the seminar collection.
cards.status_note: Reported resolution: arXiv:2607.11413v1 (13 July 2026), Theorem 1.1, states a deterministic near-linear construction meeting the source’s constant-factor target. The target correspondence, concluding proof and handling of unknown optimum were checked on 14 September 2026, but the full technical proof was not independently verified and no accepted publication of this particular result was confirmed. Status remains uncertain to express that verification limit; it should not be read as a newly certified open problem.

cards.definitions: The vertices are labelled \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), all edges are unweighted unordered pairs of distinct vertices, and the input has no repeated edges. A spanning tree is a connected acyclic graph with vertex set \([n]\) and edge set contained in \(E\); it has exactly \(n-1\) edges. Its degree counts incident tree edges. The minimum defining \(\Delta^\star(G)\) exists because the graph is finite and connected; for \(n\ge2\), it is at least one. Input is an explicit adjacency-list array with vertex offsets, an entry for each endpoint of each edge, and the integers \(n,m\); each identifier or offset occupies one word. Output is an explicit list of the tree’s \(n-1\) endpoint pairs. The algorithm is a single finite program independent of \(n,m\), with words of \(W=\lceil d\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits for a fixed integer \(d\ge4\). Each operation reads or writes constantly many addressed words, compares, branches, performs Boolean operations or shifts, adds, subtracts or multiplies modulo \(2^W\), or divides unsigned words by a nonzero divisor with quotient and remainder. Shifts by at least \(W\) return zero. Work memory initially contains zero. All input access, initialization performed by the program, preprocessing, addressing and output writes are charged; no oracle for the optimum, graph-dependent advice, real arithmetic or random coins is available. The time bound is worst-case for every valid input. Near-linear means the displayed bound with one fixed logarithmic exponent; the approximation factor is one universal constant, not a function of \(n\), \(m\) or the optimum. The deterministic convention makes explicit the type of algorithm in the currently reported resolution.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean establishing the algorithmic existence statement with explicit finite program, approximation constant and time-bound constants, or proving its negation. An affirmative proof must cover every connected input graph and produce the tree itself, without being given \(\Delta^\star(G)\). An estimate of the optimum, a guarantee restricted to dense graphs or large optimal degree, or an additive error growing with \(n\) does not by itself establish a universal constant ratio. This yes/no question does not ask to optimize \(K\) or approximate the integer optimum within \(1/100\). A cited theorem or an unformalized implementation is not a Lean-verified submission.

context_blocks.text: Saranurak’s question in Seminar 24471 concerns one input graph. It asks for a near-linear-time algorithm achieving a constant multiplicative approximation to the minimum possible maximum tree degree. Its occurrence in a seminar about distributed and dynamic algorithms does not add update operations to this particular question.

The classical Fürer–Raghavachari result has additive error at most one, but its \(O(mn)\)-scale running time is much larger than near-linear. Later near-linear constructions allowed additive terms logarithmic in the number of vertices; such terms do not yield a uniform constant ratio when the optimal degree is small.

Bhattacharya, Farokhnejad and Wang’s STOC 2026 result gives an additive-one approximation in \(\widetilde O(mn^{3/4})\) time. It improves the earlier construction time without itself meeting the near-linear target.

The July 2026 preprint by Bhattacharya, Farokhnejad, Saranurak and Wang states a deterministic construction with degree at most \(\lceil(1+\varepsilon)\Delta^\star\rceil+1\) in \(\widetilde O(m/\varepsilon^2)\) time. Its Theorem 1.1 explicitly identifies this as resolving the constant-factor question. For any fixed positive \(\varepsilon\le1\), this degree guarantee implies a universal constant factor because \(\Delta^\star\ge1\).

The preprint’s theorem, concluding proof and treatment of unknown optimum were inspected. Its full collection of technical lemmas and data-structure proofs has not been independently verified in this review, and the checked author record presents it as an arXiv manuscript. The card therefore records a reported resolution with uncertain verification status, rather than asserting that a new open gap remains or certifying a completed proof.

cards.title: Polynomial kernels for minor-free edge deletion
cards.formal: Does every fixed finite family \(\mathcal H\) of finite simple undirected graphs admit a deterministic polynomial kernel for \(\mathcal H\)-Minor-Free Edge Deletion, parameterized only by the number \(k\) of edges that may be deleted? An instance is a finite simple undirected graph \(G\) and an integer \(k\ge0\). It is a yes-instance if there exists \(F\subseteq E(G)\) with \(|F|\le k\) such that \(G-F\) contains no graph from \(\mathcal H\) as a minor. The kernel must return one equivalent instance of this same problem with total encoding length and output parameter bounded by a polynomial in \(k+1\), as specified below.
cards.why: A polynomial kernel would bound all information relevant to the deletion decision by a polynomial in the allowed number of changes, irrespective of the size of the original graph. This would make minor exclusion a broad source of effective preprocessing for edge repair. The distinction from vertex deletion matters because deleting a few edges can leave all vertices present and does not provide the same structural control as removing a small set of vertices.
cards.status_note: Explicitly open in the 2020 source and retained in the 2023 published survey. Bounded later-work checks through 2026-09-15 did not identify a deterministic polynomial kernel for every fixed forbidden-minor family, or an unconditional refutation. Existing vertex-deletion kernels and algorithms assuming minor-free inputs have different scopes.

sentences: The problem deletes at most k edges so that the remaining graph excludes every member of a fixed forbidden-minor family.
It asks whether every such family permits a polynomial-time reduction to one equivalent instance of polynomial size in k.
The input graph is arbitrary, and all vertices remain available during edge deletion.
A general kernel would provide a broad preprocessing guarantee for structural graph repair beyond known fixed-parameter algorithms.
The card restores the family quantifier and distinguishes vertex deletion, promised minor-free inputs and more general compressions.

cards.definitions: A graph \(H\) is a minor of \(G\) if it can be obtained by deleting vertices, deleting edges and contracting edges; after contraction, loops are discarded and parallel edges are merged. These operations define containment only. In the deletion problem itself, the permitted modifications are deletions of original edges: \(G-F\) retains every vertex. A graph is \(\mathcal H\)-minor-free when no \(H\in\mathcal H\) is its minor. Families and their graphs may be disconnected; no member is required to be planar. The empty family and empty graphs are allowed under the stated minor definition, including their trivial cases. The family is fixed before the input graph and budget and is not counted as an input parameter. Graph \(G\) has labelled vertices \([n]\), possibly \(n=0\), and is encoded by a length-delimited binary integer \(n\) and its upper-triangular adjacency-bit array. The budget is a length-delimited binary integer \(k\); let \(L\) be the total input bit length. A polynomial kernel for fixed \(\mathcal H\) means that there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A_{\mathcal H}\), constants \(C_{\mathcal H}\ge1\), and integers \(b_{\mathcal H},d_{\mathcal H}\ge1\) such that for every \((G,k)\) it outputs a graph \(G^{\prime}\) and integer \(k^{\prime}\ge0\) in at most \(C_{\mathcal H}(L+2)^{b_{\mathcal H}}\) bit steps, with \[(G,k)\text{ is yes}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ (G^{\prime},k^{\prime})\text{ is yes},\qquad |\operatorname{enc}(G^{\prime},k^{\prime})|+k^{\prime}\le C_{\mathcal H}(k+1)^{d_{\mathcal H}}.\] The output uses the same graph and budget encoding and the same fixed forbidden family. The machine has a fixed finite number of tapes and a finite alphabet, with initially blank work tapes; input, output and all preprocessing are charged. No randomness, oracle, graph-dependent advice, extra weights or annotations, or calls to an instance-solving oracle are allowed. Constants and the finite program may depend on the entire fixed family, but not on \(G\) or \(k\); a uniform procedure compiling an arbitrary family into its kernel is not additionally required. Input graphs have no promise of being minor-free initially. The parameter bound includes \(k=0\) through \(k+1\). Binary encoding of very large budgets does not authorize time polynomial in their numerical value; the task has only \(|E(G)|\) possible edge deletions, so budgets above this value are equivalent to that capped budget.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universally quantified kernel-existence statement, or of its negation. An affirmative proof must establish a finite deterministic polynomial-time kernel for every fixed finite forbidden family, together with the equivalence and size/parameter bounds on every input. A negative proof must establish failure for at least one specified fixed family. A result for a family containing a planar graph alone, a vertex-deletion kernel, a kernel on already minor-free input graphs, a randomized compression, or a polynomial Turing kernel does not establish the full target. A kernel with output in a different annotated or weighted problem does not suffice unless the conversion to the stated unweighted problem and its size bound are proved. Conditional lower bounds remain conditional unless their additional assumptions are proved. This is a yes/no preprocessing question, not an estimate of the optimum deletion count.

context_blocks.text: The survey’s notation uses a family of forbidden graphs, not just one forbidden graph. Its Open Problem 2.13 follows the separate planar-deletion question and concerns removing edges to obtain a minor-free graph. The card restores that family scope and uses minor containment, which is distinct from the induced-subgraph containment discussed elsewhere in the survey.

The source records fixed-parameter tractability for the deletion task, but asks for the stronger polynomial-kernel property. An algorithm with an arbitrary parameter-dependent factor can decide small-budget instances without providing a polynomial-size equivalent instance in polynomial input time.

The 2023 published survey retains Open Problem 2.13. It contrasts the edge problem with kernels for deleting vertices when the forbidden family includes a planar graph. Those vertex results neither remove the edge-versus-vertex distinction nor cover every forbidden family required here.

A kernel must preserve the decision on arbitrary input graphs, including graphs that already satisfy the target property and those far from it. It is not enough to assume the input is minor-free or to return a list of oracle queries. Changes to the graph representation, allowable modifications or parameter must be included in the equivalence and size proof.

The 2025 robust contraction-decomposition result obtains algorithms for several deletion and cut problems on graphs that are already minor-free. Here minor-freeness is the desired output property after modifications, so that result’s input restriction describes a different task and does not settle the kernel question.

cards.title: ETH barrier to single-exponential treewidth computation
cards.formal: Assuming the deterministic Exponential-Time Hypothesis (ETH) defined below, is an exact single-exponential parameterized algorithm for Treewidth impossible? Specifically, let \(\mathrm{FastTW}\) mean that there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A\), constants \(C\ge1\), and integers \(a,b\ge1\) such that, for every simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(n\ge1\) vertices and every integer \(0\le k<n\), \(A(G,k)\) decides whether \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\le k\) correctly within \(C\,2^{ak}(n+2)^b\) steps. Under the assumption ETH, determine whether \(\neg\mathrm{FastTW}\) or \(\mathrm{FastTW}\) holds. This selects the explicit single-exponential example in the source’s broader request for lower bounds.
cards.why: Treewidth is a central measure of how close a graph is to a tree, and a decomposition is often the prerequisite for running efficient parameterized algorithms. The cost of finding the optimum can therefore dominate the cost of using the structure. Establishing whether a single-exponential dependence is compatible with ETH would locate a major boundary between structural preprocessing and algorithms that work once a decomposition is already known.
cards.status_note: The 2014 source explicitly asks whether ETH excludes a single-exponential parameterized exact algorithm. The checked 2023 upper bound has quadratic parameter dependence in the exponent, while Bonnet’s 2025/2026 lower bound excludes subexponential dependence but not single-exponential dependence. Bounded checks through 2026-09-15 did not locate a resolution of this remaining conditional question.

progress.text: Bodlaender poses the explicit ETH question about exact single-exponential parameter dependence in Seminar 14451, Section 4.7, printed page 18.
Korhonen and Lokshtanov’s STOC 2023 result gives exact treewidth in \(2^{O(k^2)}n^{O(1)}\) time. The checked arXiv version 2 is dated 17 August 2023.

Bonnet’s arXiv version 2 proves the ETH-tight exponential lower bound in the vertex count and explicitly leaves the gap to quadratic parameter dependence in the exponent. This is not a super-single-exponential parameter lower bound.

The Journal of the ACM posts Bonnet’s accepted manuscript; the publisher records acceptance on 19 July 2026. These publication dates concern the established exponential lower bound, not a new resolution of the single-exponential parameter question.

cards.definitions: A tree decomposition of \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite nonempty tree \(T\) together with bags \(B_t\subseteq V\) for \(t\in V(T)\), such that every graph vertex belongs to some bag, every edge has both endpoints in one bag, and for each \(v\in V\) the set \(\{t:v\in B_t\}\) induces a connected subtree. Its width is \(\max_t|B_t|-1\), and \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\) is the minimum width over all decompositions. Graphs may be disconnected, with isolated vertices. Their input representation is the binary integer \(n\), the upper-triangular adjacency-bit array on labelled vertices \([n]\), and the binary integer \(k\), using length-delimited fields. The task is exact decision on every input, including graphs with treewidth larger than \(k\); there is no supplied decomposition or promise that the answer is yes. A Turing machine has a fixed finite number of tapes over a fixed finite alphabet, a read-only input tape, initially blank work tapes and a binary output. Each transition moves each head by at most one cell, and all input processing is charged. Programs and constants are uniform in both \(n\) and \(k\); no advice, randomness, oracle or unbounded-precision unit-cost operation is available. The single-exponential class here allows arbitrary constant polynomial factors in \(n\). ETH means that there exists a real \(\delta>0\) such that no deterministic machine in this model decides every 3-CNF formula \(F\) in time \(C\,2^{\delta N}(L+2)^b\) for any fixed \(C\ge1\) and integer \(b\ge1\). Here \(N\ge1\) is the number of Boolean variables, \(L\) is the full binary encoding length, and each clause is a disjunction of at most three literals, each literal being a variable or its negation. The input gives \(N\) in unary and the clauses as length-delimited lists of signed binary variable indices; repeated clauses are permitted. The treewidth and ETH time bounds are worst-case. Exponential dependence on the parameter alone is the target, distinct from an exponential dependence on the entire vertex count.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean, with ETH as the explicit assumption, of either \(\neg\mathrm{FastTW}\) or \(\mathrm{FastTW}\). A proof of impossibility must rule out every constant \(a,b,C\) and every uniform machine meeting the full exact decision specification. A constructive answer must supply such a machine and prove the bound and correctness; an unconditional construction is sufficient for that direction. cards.definitions: A parameterized decision problem Q is a subset of \(\{0,1\}*\times N\), with input \((x,k), n=|x|\) and k supplied in binary. XNLP consists of those Q decided by one nondeterministic multitape Turing machine using time \(g(k)(n+2)^{a}\) and working space \(g(k)\log _{2}(n+2)\) for some total computable g and constant a, simultaneously on every branch. An input is accepted exactly when some branch accepts; all branches halt within the bound. The input tape is read-only and excluded from working space, which counts visited cells on the fixed finite-alphabet work tapes. A parameterized logspace reduction \(Q_{1}\le Q_{2}\) is a deterministic halting transducer mapping \((x,k)\) to \((y,k' )\), preserving the yes/no answer, with \(k' \le h(k)\) for a total computable h and space \(h(k)+C \log _{2}(n+2)\) for an absolute C. Its output is write-only and is not counted as working space. Q is XNLP-hard when every problem in XNLP has such a reduction to Q. In the conjectured forbidden deterministic algorithm there is no randomness, oracle or advice, and a single program handles all parameters. Constants, including c and the code computing f, are fixed for that program; f may grow arbitrarily fast but must be computable. Using different computable functions in the time and space bounds is equivalent, since one common f can dominate both. Replacing n by \(n+2\) only handles short inputs. Slice-wise polynomial time allows its exponent to depend on k; the conjectured space bound permits dependence on k only in a multiplicative factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the simultaneous resource obstruction for every XNLP-hard problem, or refute it by an XNLP-hard problem and one uniform deterministic algorithm satisfying both bounds for explicit computable f and fixed c. A space bound achieved by a different algorithm, a time bound with a superpolynomial exponent in n at fixed k, or a result for only bounded parameter values does not meet the criterion.

cards.title: Disjoint-union closure of tractable forbidden patterns
cards.formal: For every pair of fixed nonempty finite simple graphs \(H_{1},H_{2}\), is the following implication true? If Independent Set parameterized by the requested set size k is fixed-parameter tractable on \(H_{1}\)-free graphs and is fixed-parameter tractable on \(H_{2}\)-free graphs, then it is fixed-parameter tractable on \((H_{1}\sqcup H_{2})\)-free graphs. Here exclusion is as an induced subgraph, ⊔ is disjoint union of the forbidden patterns, and fixed-parameter tractability has the deterministic meaning defined below. The two forbidden graphs may themselves be disconnected and may be isomorphic.
cards.why: A closure theorem would reduce the classification of parameterized Independent Set with one forbidden induced pattern to its connected components. It would organize many currently separate tractability results through one general structural principle.

cards.definitions: For a fixed graph H, an input to Independent Set on H-free graphs is a finite simple undirected graph G on n labeled vertices, encoded by its adjacency matrix, and a binary integer k with \(0\le k\le n\), under the promise that no subset of \(V(G)\) induces a graph isomorphic to H. The answer is YES exactly when there is a set \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with |\(S|\ge k\) and no edge between distinct members of S. Only k is the parameter; H is fixed in the definition of the restricted problem and is not supplied as a variable-size input. Call H tractable if there exist a deterministic algorithm \(A_{H}, a\) total computable function \(f_{H}:\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\) and a constant \(c_{H}\ge 0\) such that \(A_{H}\) correctly decides every promised input in at most \(f_{H}(k)(n+1)^{c_{H}}\) bit operations. The algorithm is uniform over n,k and its guarantees are worst-case and exact. Behavior outside the H-free promise is unrestricted. Constants, algorithms and computable functions may depend on H, while \(c_{H}\) cannot depend on k or n. For \(H_{1}\sqcup H_{2}\) take disjoint copies of their vertex sets, preserve the edges within each copy, and put no edges between copies. Thus a graph contains an induced \(H_{1}\sqcup H_{2}\) precisely when it has disjoint induced copies of \(H_{1}\) and \(H_{2}\) with no cross-edge between them. Excluding this one disconnected pattern is weaker than simultaneously excluding both \(H_{1}\) and \(H_{2}\). The conjecture says that the set of tractable forbidden patterns is closed under ⊔. Its quantifier is over existence of algorithms for each fixed pair; it does not additionally demand one effective transformation that constructs an algorithm from descriptions of \(H_{1},H_{2}\) or from the two assumed algorithms. Input graphs G are not promised to be disconnected. Weighted Independent Set and randomized fixed-parameter algorithms define different variants; this card uses the source’s unqualified deterministic FPT convention.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed \(H_{1},H_{2}\) satisfying the two tractability premises there exist an algorithm A, a computable f and a constant c, all allowed to depend on that pair, deciding the \((H_{1}\sqcup H_{2})\)-free problem in \(f(k)(n+1)^{c}\) time; or refute this universal implication. A refutation must establish both premises and failure of the conclusion for its pair. A \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hardness proof for the conclusion is only a conditional refutation unless the relevant FPT-versus-\(\mathrm{W}[1]\) separation is assumed explicitly. A result for the intersection of the two graph classes or for disjoint input components does not settle this statement.

cards.definitions:
A problem instance I has an explicitly represented finite universe U and a parameter k≥1. Its witnesses form a family W(I,k) of k-element subsets of U, not a family of ordered tuples or of certificates attached to the same subset. For example, when a witness is a k-vertex set supporting a path, several paths on that same vertex set do not create several witnesses. Each output is one subset, represented by its sorted list of element indices. The output order among subsets is unrestricted. Let N=|W(I,k)|; the algorithm is not given N. Instances with k>|U| have no witnesses.

“Self-contained” means that restricting the instance to X⊆U preserves exactly the witnesses contained in X: W(I|X,k)={W∈W(I,k):W⊆X}. The restriction examines only the retained elements and their relationships, is computable in polynomial time, and has encoded length polynomial in the original length L. A decision procedure on I|X therefore answers whether X contains a witness of the original instance. This is the inclusion query INC(I,X,k). Witnesses whose validity depends on their relationships to deleted elements, such as a vertex cover of the original graph, do not automatically satisfy this property.

The premise is a deterministic algorithm deciding whether W(I,k) is nonempty in time g(k)L^a, for some computable g and constant a independent of k and I. It thus also implements inclusion queries with an FPT bound. The desired enumerator may depend on the fixed witness problem, as may f and its constant polynomial exponent, but all of them must be uniform over its instances and parameter values. This is an implication between algorithmic existence statements; it does not additionally require an effective compiler from arbitrary decision-program code, or restrict the enumerator to a black-box oracle.

For a fixed input, let τ_i be the time when the ith distinct witness has finished being written, τ₀=0, and τ_{N+1} the termination time. Expected FPT delay requires E[τ_{i+1}−τ_i]≤f(k)(L+1)^b for every i=0,…,N, with a constant b independent of k,I,i,N. When N=0 it bounds the whole time to termination. Expectation is over the internal randomness on this fixed input, without conditioning on a particular random execution history. The algorithm never outputs a false or duplicate witness and finishes the complete list with probability one. Its bound charges all work, including any preprocessing, inclusion-query execution, duplicate handling and writing outputs. The question imposes no additional polynomial-space requirement.

An expected-incremental-FPT bound instead allows E[τ_{i+1}−τ_i]≤h(k)(L+i+1)^c, which grows with the number already output. An expected-output-FPT bound controls only the final expected time by h(k)(L+N+1)^c. Such a total bound may conceal a long wait before the next output. Dropping “expected” requires the corresponding deterministic bound. These notions are not identified with each other here. An extension query additionally asks whether some witness W satisfies Y⊆W⊆X for a prescribed Y; the premise provides no such forced-inclusion operation.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated implication for all self-contained k-witness problems, or exhibit a problem satisfying its decision premise and prove that no enumerator with the stated expected-delay guarantee exists, with any complexity assumption made explicit. A bound only on final expected running time, a delay allowed to grow polynomially with the number already output, a randomized list that can omit witnesses, or a result assuming an efficient extension oracle does not settle this selected branch. The source’s deterministic and incremental companion questions require separate conclusions.

cards.title: Polynomial kernels for forbidden-minor vertex deletion
cards.formal: Does vertex deletion to exclude any fixed finite family of graph minors admit a polynomial kernel, parameterized by the number of vertices allowed to be deleted? cards.definitions:
The family \(\mathcal F\) is fixed before inputs are supplied; it is not part of the parameterized input. Its members are finite nonempty undirected graphs and may be disconnected. The original source allows parallel edges, as in its two-vertex examples. Use finite undirected loopless multigraphs with all edge copies explicitly listed for the general convention here; simple graphs are included.

A graph \(H\) is a minor of \(G\) if it can be obtained from a subgraph by contracting edges. Contraction identifies their endpoints, removes resulting loops and retains parallel edges. It is not induced-subgraph containment or topological-minor containment.

The input consists of \(G\) and a nonnegative integer \(k\). It is a yes-instance if there is \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with \(|S|\leq k\) such that \(G-S\) contains no member of \(\mathcal F\) as a minor. All vertices have unit deletion cost. There is no planarity, degree, connectivity or sparsity promise on \(G\). The empty forbidden family is trivial and may be omitted. Since every forbidden graph is nonempty, \(k\geq |V(G)|\) is immediately a yes-instance.

A polynomial kernel is a deterministic algorithm that runs in a polynomial in the total binary input length and outputs a single pair \((G^{\prime},k^{\prime})\) for the same fixed family. It must preserve the yes/no answer exactly on every input. There must be constants \(C_{\mathcal F},c_{\mathcal F}\) such that the total bit length of the output and the numerical value \(k'\) are at most \(C_{\mathcal F}(k+1)^{c_{\mathcal F}}\). Vertex labels can be renumbered. Counting only vertices while leaving arbitrarily many explicit parallel edges or a large encoded parameter would not suffice.

The algorithm, its polynomial running-time degree and the output exponent may depend on \(\mathcal F\). The question does not require one exponent that works for all families, nor an effective procedure constructing the kernel algorithm from an arbitrary family description. Such uniformity requirements would strengthen the target.

The parameter is the solution budget \(k\). It is not the size of a supplied vertex cover, a set whose removal leaves bounded treedepth, or another structural parameter. A kernel supplies one smaller equivalent instance, unlike an algorithm querying many small instances. Approximate kernels that lose a constant factor in deletion cost do not satisfy the exact equivalence requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a polynomial kernel for every fixed finite forbidden family in this solution-budget model, allowing family-dependent exponents, or establish that some fixed family does not admit one. A conventional lower bound of the form “a polynomial kernel would imply NP is contained in coNP/poly” must retain that complexity assumption and is a conditional obstruction, not an unconditional separation. Special-family algorithms and approximate or structural-parameter kernels alone do not establish the universal claim.

cards.title: Polynomial kernels for Directed Feedback Vertex Set
cards.formal:
Does Directed Feedback Vertex Set admit a deterministic polynomial kernel parameterized solely by the deletion budget? More precisely, do there exist a deterministic algorithm \(K\), constants \(C,c>0\), and a polynomial \(p\), such that for every finite digraph \(D\) and nonnegative integer \(k\), \(K\) runs in at most \(p(L)\) steps on the explicit input of bit length \(L\), and outputs one instance \((D^{\prime},k^{\prime})\) of the same problem satisfying
\[
D\text{ has a directed feedback vertex set of size at most }k
\iff
D^{\prime}\text{ has one of size at most }k^{\prime},
\]
with the entire output encoding having at most \(C(k+1)^{c}\) bits? The constants and algorithm must work for all inputs. No additional structural parameter or promise on the input or the remaining acyclic graph is permitted.

references.authors: Mnich, Matthias; van Leeuwen, Erik Jan

cards.definitions:
A digraph \(D=(V,A)\) has a finite explicitly listed vertex set and an arc set \(A\subseteq V\times V\). Self-loops and opposite arcs are allowed; repeated copies of an arc have no effect and need not be represented. A directed cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices \(v_{0},\ldots,v_{r-1}\), with \(r\ge1\), having arcs from each vertex to the next, including from \(v_{r-1}\) to \(v_{0}\). Thus a self-loop is a cycle and two opposite arcs form a cycle.

A directed feedback vertex set is a subset \(S\subseteq V\) such that the induced digraph \(D[V\setminus S]\) has no directed cycle. The decision instance is YES exactly when some such set has \(|S|\le k\). The remaining graph may be any directed acyclic graph, including a disconnected one.

Encode vertices by integers \(1,\ldots,n\), list all vertices and arcs, and encode \(k\) in binary using a fixed ordinary self-delimiting binary encoding. Measure preprocessing time on a deterministic multitape Turing machine in the total input length \(L\). The output uses the same encoding, with newly numbered vertices and a nonnegative binary integer \(k^{\prime}\). Bounding only the number of output vertices while permitting arbitrarily much auxiliary information would not meet the stated size requirement.

A kernel preserves the YES/NO answer, not necessarily the optimum value, the original vertex labels, or every solution. The output budget may differ from the input budget. The requirement is a single small instance of this same unweighted decision problem; a list of oracle queries or a compression into a different language is a different notion.

The preprocessing time must be polynomial in \(L\), uniformly for all \(k\). A procedure taking \(f(k)L^{d}\) time for an unrestricted computable function \(f\) is not by itself a polynomial-time kernelization. The case \(k=0\) is covered by the bound \(C(k+1)^{c}\). Allowing loops makes the model explicit and does not change the question: each loop forces its vertex into any deletion set, while repeated arcs can be removed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of an algorithm with the stated uniform polynomial preprocessing, exact answer equivalence, and polynomial output bit bound depending only on the original deletion budget, or refute that existence. A conditional lower bound must state its complexity assumption explicitly; it is not an unconditional refutation. A kernel using a larger structural parameter does not settle this target.

context_blocks.text: The source proves polynomial kernels when deletion must leave an out-tree, an out-forest, or a directed pumpkin. These are stronger conditions than merely destroying directed cycles, so the results do not constitute a kernel for general Directed Feedback Vertex Set.

context_blocks.title: Later kernels use additional structure
context_blocks.text: The WADS 2019 result, subsequently published in the 2025 journal article, gives a polynomial kernel with parameter \(k+\ell\), where \(\ell\) is the size of a supplied vertex set whose removal leaves an underlying undirected graph of fixed bounded treewidth. Here treewidth at most \(\eta\) means that there are vertex bags indexed by a tree, each of size at most \(\eta+1\), covering all vertices and both endpoints of every edge, with the bags containing each vertex forming a connected subtree. The constant \(\eta\) is fixed. The extra \(\ell\) need not be bounded by a polynomial in \(k\); the general question therefore remains distinct.

context_blocks.title: The parameter in a negative result also matters
context_blocks.text: The same work distinguishes the combined parameter \(k+\ell\) from parameterization by \(\ell\) alone. Its conditional obstruction for the latter does not rule out a polynomial kernel in the solution budget \(k\).
